name: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso)

card.summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor gel approved in 2013 for facial redness in rosacea; it works within hours but is temporary, and rebound redness has been reported.
card.note: Case reports describe rebound or paradoxical redness, allergic contact dermatitis and, rarely, bradycardia.

quick.overview:
Mirvaso is a 0.33% brimonidine tartrate gel that the FDA approved in 2013 for the facial redness of rosacea. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist also used in eye drops for glaucoma and for eye redness.

It is discussed as a temporary redness reducer that narrows skin blood vessels, with an effect that peaks within hours of application. Published case reports also describe rebound or worsened redness in some users.
quick.mechanism: Brimonidine activates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the skin's blood vessels, causing them to constrict and reducing visible redness. Rosacea overviews place this effect at roughly 3 to 6 hours after application.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include flushing or redness worse than baseline, allergic contact dermatitis, severe rebound erythema in case reports, and one reported case of symptomatic bradycardia. It is prescription-only in many countries.

lead: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso, brimonidine tartrate 0.33%) was approved by the US FDA in 2013 for facial erythema of rosacea and was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition [7][9]. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, first patented in 1972 and in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions [7].

For appearance, the point is temporary reduction of visible facial redness. Brimonidine narrows the small blood vessels of the skin, so a flushed or persistently red face looks more even for several hours after a single application. It does not treat the underlying condition; Wikipedia's rosacea article says medications often give a temporary remission of redness that usually returns when treatment stops.[16]

Rosacea overviews describe brimonidine as constricting vessels to reduce redness, with a peak effect 3 to 6 hours after application [7]. A review of facial erythema in rosacea places the redness in the context of immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction [1].
Published case reports describe adverse reactions including allergic contact dermatitis [2][5], rebound erythema [6][3] and a case of symptomatic bradycardia [8].
infobox: Peak effect about 3 to 6 hours after application[7]

paras: Mirvaso is a clear gel containing 0.33% brimonidine tartrate, applied to the face once daily for persistent redness in adults with rosacea.[7][9] Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist; the same molecule is used in eye drops for glaucoma and, at lower concentrations, in drops sold for eye redness.[7]

Rosacea is a common, chronic facial skin condition with persistent redness, flushing, visible vessels and sometimes bumps. Wikipedia reports estimates of 1 to 10% of people affected, more often fair-skinned people, with triggers that include sunlight, temperature extremes, alcohol, hot drinks, spicy foods, exercise and stress.[16] Persistent facial redness was long considered difficult to treat directly, and brimonidine was described at launch as targeting it specifically.[9][10]

The gel is indicated for persistent facial redness of rosacea in adults [3][7]. The same ingredient appears in ophthalmic products for glaucoma and ocular redness, some available over the counter in the US [7].

A 2014 Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin appraisal and a SkinMed product summary reviewed the product at launch [9][10]. A small imaging study used optical coherence tomography to monitor treatment response [4]. Registered post-marketing studies include open-label studies of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey [11][12][13]; results are not summarised here. Because the effect is a vessel constriction, rosacea references describe it as reducing redness during the hours of effect rather than altering the disease [7].

A multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study of brimonidine gel 0.33% reported rapid improvement in patient-reported outcomes of facial erythema.[17] Medical Letter reviews in 2013 and 2024 summarise brimonidine among the topical options for rosacea redness, alongside oxymetazoline and treatments for the bumps and pimples of rosacea.[19][20] Laser and intense pulsed light, which target visible vessels rather than general flushing, are a separate approach described in encyclopaedic summaries.[16]

Commonly reported adverse events include redness or flushing worse than baseline, most often with the first application [3]. Case reports describe a paradoxical erythema reaction with long-term use [3], severe rebound erythema labelled dermatitis medicamentosa [6], and allergic contact dermatitis, including sensitisation in two cases [2][5]. A 2024 case report described symptomatic bradycardia after use [8]. Systemic effects of brimonidine in other forms include low blood pressure and dry mouth [7].
Brimonidine constricts blood vessels through alpha-2 adrenergic activation, which in the skin reduces redness [7].

Rosacea reviews describe the redness as arising from immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction, with dilated cutaneous vessels; brimonidine acts on the vessel wall rather than on those upstream processes.[1][7] Wikipedia lists the peak improvement at three to six hours after application.[16] Oxymetazoline cream, a related alpha-agonist approved later, is covered in its own entry.[18]

Human studies include open-label post-marketing trials in rosacea [11][12], a utilisation study [13] and a small imaging study [4]. Studies in other conditions (hand-foot syndrome, flushing in aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency) are registered but concern other uses [14][15].

The pivotal-type evidence includes the randomised, vehicle-controlled JEADV study of patient-reported outcomes.[17] A randomised trial in Asian individuals tested topical brimonidine against alcohol-induced facial flushing, a use outside rosacea.[21] Registered post-marketing studies of Mirvaso include open-label trials of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey.[11][12][13]
The gel is mentioned in skincare circles as an option for temporary redness before events, typically alongside discussion of rebound redness reports.

Users who mention it describe it as a short-lived corrector, applied before a photo or event, in the same conversation as green-tinted concealer, sunscreen and trigger avoidance. Reports of rebound redness are part of how the product is discussed, and the case-report literature describes the same reaction.[3][6]

The gel was approved by the US FDA in 2013 and is a prescription product in many countries, while brimonidine eye drops for redness are sold over the counter in some markets.[7] Case reports of allergic reactions, paradoxical redness, severe rebound and bradycardia are the basis for the cautions discussed in clinical reviews.[2][3][5][6][8]

timeline.event: FDA approves Mirvaso gel 0.33% for facial erythema of rosacea.[7]
